article.plain_text:
Most people give their Grok bot one job: everything
Research. Ideas. Code. Launch copy
Then the bot fails
So they rewrite the prompt
They add rules in CAPS LOCK
They paste a 3,000-word "master instruction"
The bot still invents numbers
It still skips the tests
It still says DONE when nothing is done
The problem is not Grok
The problem is everything around Grok
That layer has a name: the harness
And on Grok Bot, you build it yourself
The prompt tells the bot what to doThe harness decides what it can actually get away with
A Grok bot is a brain with a computer strapped to it
Every bot on Grok Bot is a persistent teammate
Its own cloud computer. Its own terminal and browser. Files that stay after you close your laptop. A schedule it can wake up on
That is real power
Power without structure is just expensive chaos
 
Put Grok in a chat box and it answers questions
Put the same Grok inside a folder with rules, files, checks and a schedule and it ships products
The weights didn't change
The harness did
 
Why one mega-bot always rots
The first instinct is one super-bot with a giant prompt
It works for a day
Then the context fills up with research, opinions, half-written code and old decisions
And the bot starts mixing all of it together
 
The researcher should never invent a business model
The builder should never invent requirements that aren't in the spec
One bot doing ten jobs is the bug. Ten bots doing one job each is the system
The 6 layers of a Grok Bot harness
This is the whole framework
Build it top to bottom. Each layer removes one way to fail
 
1. Turn the request into a contract
Never give a bot a vibe
Give it a bounded object
 
Without done_when, the bot decides what "done" means
It will always pick the easiest version
2. Give it a map, not a manual
Don't paste every doc into every bot
Put one small guide at the root of the workspace that says where things live
 
A map saves context
A giant manual eats it
3. Give every bot a lane
Tool access is not a list of buttons
It's a permission boundary
 
One input file. One output file. One job
If a bot needs to do two things, you need two bots
4. Memory lives in files, not in the chat
The chat is not your database
Grok Bot keeps /workspace when the bot's computer rebuilds itself. Anything outside it can disappear
So state goes there
 
Bots don't talk to each other
They pass files
Each bot reads the file before it, writes its own, then adds one line to HANDOFF.md
 
 
5. Sensors before autonomy
A bot can't fix what it can't see
Before you give it more freedom, give it more evidence
 
The bot makes the artifact
The checks produce evidence
The harness decides if that evidence is enough
6. Permissions and receipts live outside the model
The bot can suggest an action
It must never approve its own action
 
And every run ends with a receipt, not just an output
 
A clean final answer can hide a broken process
A receipt can't
The loop belongs to the harness, not the bot
"Keep trying until it works" is not a plan
It's a slot machine
Put the loop in the rules:
 
The bot decides how to fix the gap
The harness decides whether it gets another try
Every failure should upgrade the system
Most people fix the output
Harness builders fix the class of failure
 
 
A patch fixes one run
A rule fixes every run after it
That's the compounding advantage
A good harness turns bot mistakes into infrastructure
The shared rules block
Paste it at the top of every bot's instructions
It's what keeps the team from going rogue
 
The approval rule matters more than it looks
The bots do the work. You keep the trigger
Routines: let the schedule be the boss
Grok Bot can run bots on a schedule
Which means the harness keeps working when you're not there
 
Keep scheduled scans small and sharp
Public sources have rate limits. Fewer good queries beat a hundred spammy ones
Start with the smallest harness that closes the loop
You don't need a nine-bot empire on day one
 
Move up only when the task earns it
A one-off research question needs Level 0
A bot that writes code on a schedule needs Level 3
The Grok Bot harness checklist
Before you trust a bot with real work, ask:
 
If several answers are no, a smarter model won't save you
It will just fail faster and sound more confident
The real shift
Prompt engineering tells the bot what to do
Context engineering decides what the bot sees
Harness engineering builds the world the bot works in
 
Grok will get smarter next month
Your rules, files, checks and gates keep their value either way
The people shipping fastest don't have the smartest bot. They have the best harness
LIKE
SUB
BOOK
BECOME LEGEND

I respect Jukan, but I feel a little frustrated whenever I see this kind of argument.

You can build any scenario around plausible assumptions, and yes, of course, the outcome will follow from those assumptions. If you assume demand collapses, customers accumulate inventory, and contract terms get renegotiated, then naturally, memory companies’ revenue and profits will decline.

But honestly, this feels like the perspective of analysts who treat memory as just a commodity you manufacture and sell, without properly understanding the technological changes taking place in custom memory.

Who exactly are these customers we are talking about when we say they could cancel LTAs or defer deliveries? They are the very customers working with memory companies to design the next generation of HBM and 3D stacked DRAM.

After jointly designing and validating these products, can customers really cancel those volumes so easily or push deliveries out by one or two years? How would they manufacture their own products, which were designed around that memory? What happens to the launch and system deployment schedules they have already coordinated? Switching suppliers also raises questions of design compatibility and requalification. If you are going to argue that contracts can be adjusted, you also need to explain what that decision would mean for the very customers canceling them.

This is one of the biggest reasons I keep saying that memory is no longer the same cyclical industry it used to be. The parties to these LTAs are already tied together from the design stage. But if you still view memory simply as a commodity where rising prices lead to more production, and inventory buildups lead to price cuts or canceled orders, you will inevitably miss this shift in the technical and business relationships.

One more thing. These arguments about a collapse in memory demand seem to assume that planned AI data center investments will be canceled on a massive scale, or that AI infrastructure expansion will slow so substantially that memory demand falls sharply. What interests me more than whether contracts can be adjusted is why you expect demand to weaken that dramatically in the first place.

I think it would be more realistic to discuss directly whether the AI era we expect will actually fail to materialize, and whether much of the AI infrastructure investment currently planned will disappear. If that is your outlook, I can at least understand why you would expect memory demand to collapse and customers to cut volumes even for products they have jointly developed.

What bravery really is, it’s actually boldly taking action in the face of overwhelming fear. 

Whether it’s helping this fight against the evil of our country or in your own personal life, do something brave today. 

What’s that look like for you? Idk, is it taking to Twitter and sharing your information like me? Is it going after that new promotion at work? Is it going after that relationship that’s risky but if it pays off could be the relationship you’ve ever had? Is it telling someone how you really feel about them? If that’s too overwhelming, maybe you should try starting smaller and building up to those bigger acts of bravery. 

If you let fear govern your life, you’ll never take the proper risks to get what you want. To get what you want, at some point you have to take a risk, be brave, and act even though you feel you’re surrounded by fear. 

At some point you have to decide, who narrates your life. Fear and the world’s opinions about you, or is it you using your actions and words to create the world you want and achieve everything you desire? 

So speak your mind. If not in the same vain as me, find out how to do this in your own life. Tell the person you are scared of rejection from how you feel. note_tweet.text:
I'd like to believe LTAs are durable too. But take one example.

Analog chipmaker onsemi said this in 2023.
On January 5, 2023, at JPMorgan's CES forum, CEO Hassane El-Khoury was asked how much LTSAs would still hold once the shortage eased. His answer: “They are a legally binding agreement ’cause they’re a liability for the customer because they’re take or pay.” He also said he would not accept a customer reopening price talks just because it could get the same parts 10% cheaper elsewhere.

On October 30, 2023, on the Q3 earnings call, onsemi cut its SiC shipment forecast for the year from $1 billion to more than $800 million after one automotive OEM reduced demand. An analyst asked how this could happen when the company had been saying its LTSAs were legally binding. The same CEO reaffirmed that they were binding, but said he did not want to enforce the contracts just to push inventory onto a customer whose demand had dropped. If it worked for both sides, terms could be adjusted customer by customer, whether by a quarter, a year, or longer.

In its 10-K filings, onsemi also states that it amended LTSAs with some strategic customers by mutual agreement in 2024, and changed delivery schedules and committed volumes on some LTSAs in 2025 as demand shifted.

Microchip is another case. Customers in its Preferred Supply Program (PSP) originally had to place 12 months of orders and could not cancel or reschedule them unless Microchip raised prices. On its November 2025 earnings call, however, the CEO said the company had accepted some cancellations and pushouts so customers could adjust their backlog. On the same call, the CFO separately addressed the multiyear LTSAs the company had signed. Some of those contracts were still in effect, he said, but customers had been allowed to defer taking delivery of committed volumes by one to two years if they needed to.

Every time I see cases like these, I doubt how much memory makers' LTAs will protect earnings in a downcycle. Right now the most reliable thing is the prepayments and deposits themselves. That cash can go into capacity expansion today.

I can picture hyperscalers with no DRAM inventory continuing to buy at current prices. But once inventory has piled up, will they keep taking every committed unit at the same price? I have a hard time picturing memory makers holding customers to the high contract price all the way through.

The LTA itself may never be broken and may stay in place. But if both sides agree to push this year's volumes into next year or two years out, this year's earnings estimates come down. If price gets renegotiated too, margin estimates have to come down as well.

Again, I agree LTAs are sturdier than they used to be. What I question is whether, after demand turns, memory makers can still earn 80% margins on contracts signed during the upturn and keep collecting hundreds of billions of dollars in profit because of those LTAs.
